### What Does Extreme Heat Do to the Body

**PBS**, *09 03, 2026*

#### Video (9:59)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/wXoqEJlsKu0?start=2 title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

#### Description

Watch more of this series: https://to.pbs.org/4wkQIAG

The climate crisis isn't a distant threat — it's already here, and it's deadly. But keeping people cool is surprisingly complicated. 

In Sydney, Australia, physiologist Ollie Jay is tackling the problem by studying how the human body responds to extreme heat. The ultimate goal is to create low-cost cooling strategies for people without access to air conditioning — those most at risk from extreme heat. Science journalist Miles O'Brien puts himself in the hot seat — literally — to find out what it feels like when the body's cooling system starts to fail.

    Jeva, there are as many as twelve thousand recorded heat deaths in The US each year. How does that how do we account for that? How do we know that people have died because of extreme heat?
    
- ##### Speaker: 400:19:42
    
    It's a complicated question. There's about three different ways you can calculate excess or, heat deaths. One is direct and indirect. These are two different categories of looking at deaths. So direct deaths from heat, there's a diagnostic code. It's x 30. It's a medical classification for a death due to excessive natural heat. This is distinct from excessive unnatural heat, such as a tanning bed death, a little bit of morbid trivia through the morning. But the direct deaths are exactly what we're talking about in terms of heat exhaustion or heat stroke. The the classic what you think of as somebody dying from heat. Then there are excess dust or indirect dust from heat. That's cardiovascular events, stroke, complications from diabetes, respiratory illness, all the other ways that heat can kill you that's maybe a little bit more invisible. So if somebody comes into a hospital with a heart attack, the physicians are treating that heart attack. They're not sitting there being like, is this heart attack from the heat outside right now? So it might not be coded as a direct heat death, but it's still somebody who died from the heat. And there's two different ways you can count these excess heat deaths. So one is to look at how many more people died compared to what you would have expected for that period of time. And then for so for an example of this is, in France, there were, twenty one thousand six hundred all cause deaths between June 17 and July 2. That was their heat wave in Europe. Statistical modeling would have expected about fifteen thousand nine hundred and ten deaths based on the previous year, so that gives us an excess of about seven or, five thousand seven hundred. And then the third way of doing this is basically a predictive model. So saying we know when the temperature rises by x amount, this number of people will die and kind of using that model to fit with, the temperatures that were recorded. So there's a bunch of different ways to record excess deaths, a bunch of different models that need to be peer reviewed. And so this this work is still ongoing for heat events, both in Europe and in North America. But this is why you can see many different numbers for how many people died in a given heat wave.

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/5tv31geSxNlyz9aGq1ivib)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2TDswhCVfRb4CNBlGEMVfM)

In this week’s podcast we’ll explore how America’s streets can be redesigned to benefit bicyclists and pedestrians—and we’ll explain why doing so may even help mitigate the effects of climate change. A new study from Anne Lusk, research scientist in the Department of Nutrition at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, analyzed how bicyclists and pedestrians responded to various placements of trees along cycle tracks—barrier-protected bicycle-exclusive paths between the road and the sidewalk. The research shows that the placement of these trees can play an important role in how people walking and biking perceive traffic, pollution, heat, and even safety. But the benefits extend beyond just those using the street—and could even be a factor in mitigating the effects of climate change. These trees may make it more likely that people will bike—helping to reduce pollution. And increased greenery can also help cool cities, which often suffer from a heat island effect, which means they’re significantly warmer than more rural areas. Lusk says all of this highlights the need to re-think how we’re designing streets to encourage more people to walk and bike instead of drive.

This is distinct from excessive unnatural heat, such as a tanning bed death, a little bit of morbid trivia through the morning. #### Climate Change and Extreme Heat End of Summer Episode with Dr. Kelly Turner and Dr. Ladd Keith

![Climate Change and Extreme Heat End of Summer Episode with Dr. Kelly Turner and Dr. Ladd Keith](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1fe59f9a339398e497c814e46f)

In episode  192 of America Adapts, Doug Parsons hosts Dr. Kelly Turner and Dr. Ladd Keith. Kelly is an Associate Professor of Urban Planning at UCLA and Ladd is an assistant professor in the School of Landscape Architecture and Planning at the University of Arizona.  We learn how extreme heat disproportionately impacts marginalized communities.  We also explore the evolving media coverage of extreme heat. The three of us break down the highs and lows of all the media coverage of extreme heat this past summer.  We also learn about Kelly's research on heat's impact on California schools, and what that means for both public health and student learning.  We take a dive into federal approaches to heat management and learn about the glaring disparity in resources and attention allocated to extreme heat compared to other climate hazards and ponder the potential for FEMA to classify extreme heat as a disaster declaration.  We also discuss the value of having a national adaptation plan for extreme heat planning. Finally, and yes, we go there, we get an update on the efforts to name heat waves. We highlight the pros and cons of this approach and discuss other options.  It is a gangbuster episode and that's just a sampling of what we cover.  Transcripts for this episode available here. (These are computer generated so pardon the errors.)  Topics Covered:    Dr. Turner specializes in heat equity research, while Dr. Keith focuses on heat policy planning and governance.  Increasing prevalence of extreme heat due to climate change and its disproportionate impact on marginalized groups.  Media coverage of extreme heat is becoming more sophisticated, highlighting impacts on workers and public health.  Dr. Turner's research in California focuses on schools and heat's impact on student learning.  Discussion of heating planning strategies including shade in urban design.  The Biden administration is updating heat safety labor laws, emphasizing the need for comprehensive regulations at state and federal levels and the potential for FEMA labeling heat events as disaster declarations.  Naming heat waves to increase public awareness is debated, highlighting the importance of reaching vulnerable populations.  Will heat lead to managed retreat from regions that become uninhabitable?  A national adaptation plan is emphasized to address heat impacts, especially for marginalized communities. Climate change will mean more extreme weather, including heat waves. And it’s not a distant threat—we’re already seeing the effects now in the United States. In this week’s episode, we explore the health threat posed by severe heat and how our society needs to adapt in the decades ahead. You'll hear from Augusta Williams, a doctoral student at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, who studies how extreme heat can affect our bodies and minds. She'll explain why heat is considered a "silent killer" and how we can combat the effects of our warming world. #### Why are scientists planting tiny forests in big cities?

**Duration:** 00:12:12

**Released:** 2026

**Series:** Short Wave

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2rTT1klKUoQNuaW2Ah19Pa)

Healthy forests help combat climate change, provide humans with drinking water and even improve mental and physical health. But it’s hard to imagine an entire forest in the middle of a big city. That’s where micro-forests come into play — public forests on a smaller scale, filled with native plants. They exist around the world, and producer Rachel Carlson went to visit the largest micro-forest in California in this encore episode. She joins host Emily Kwong to chat about what she saw. Interested in more of the science behind urban nature? #### Why Heat Waves Become Deadly

##### Presenting: The Carbon Copy – Why Heat Waves Become Deadly

![Presenting: The Carbon Copy – Why Heat Waves Become Deadly](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1fd88e9fa2e08b696116873d43)

**Series:** How to Save a Planet

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/1KzrasExlM5dgMYwgFHns6)

Today we’re sharing an episode of The Carbon Copy, a climate change podcast produced by Canary Media. The topic is extremely timely: heat waves. This summer saw extreme heat blanketing almost every region of the northern hemisphere. And these heat waves aren’t just uncomfortable or inconvenient. They’re deadly. In most years, extreme heat kills more people in the U.S. than any other weather-related disaster. This episode asks: how can we better prepare for these heat waves? Some of the answers are surprisingly simple–and they could help address problems beyond extreme heat.Check out the rest of the series on Spotify or CanaryMedia.com. Learn more about your ad choices. #### Extreme Heat Is the New Normal

**New York Times Opinion**, *08 28, 2026*

##### Video (15:42)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/QcHuAtK_H_8 title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

We filmed “A New Inferno,” the short documentary above, in Phoenix, one of the hottest cities in America, through some of the city’s hottest days of 2025, during one of the hottest years on record globally. On one of our production days, temperatures reached 118 while we were filming outside.

In the face of extreme heat, we documented firefighters and paramedics of the Phoenix Fire Department saving lives in real time. We wanted to call attention to a specialized technique of ice bag immersion for people facing life-threatening heat stroke. We hope that telling their story and showcasing the efficacy of this strategy will encourage wider adoption of this protocol across the country.

Yet this procedure is ultimately a stopgap, as firefighters do their best to adapt to the climate crisis in front of them. The underlying story of heat in Phoenix is one of broader, interlocking crises: homelessness and substance use disorders that are deeply entangled with urban heat, each amplifying the other, illustrating how climate change affects the disenfranchised most brutally.

With our film, we aim to reframe how the public thinks about heat: as an invisible, silent killer reshaping the rhythms of urban life.

Documentary and text by By Nita Blum-Reddick and Jonathan Pickett

#### Heat Wave Cooling Our Cities Without Air Conditioning

**Bloomberg Originals**, *03 08, 2023*

##### Video (12:22)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/XCAVWXHHnqg title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Humans are increasingly reliant on air conditioning, but its use contributes to global warming. As the world warms and demand rises, how can we make A/C sustainable? In Spain and India, Kal Penn explores two innovative solutions. 

---
Getting Warmer is Bloomberg's exclusive new show about climate, clean energy and business, anchored by actor and former White House aide Kal Penn.

Accompany him on his journey as he takes an up-close look at bold climate solutions and discovers new facets of the global transition to clean energy.

In a hosted studio segment, Penn sifts through the overwhelming news about our climate and breaks down the facts and trends to understand with a dose of humor and optimism. Why are the recycling symbols on your plastic cups misleading? How does the carbon credit market work and does it actually help? And what is the future of water in a drought-ridden world?

On the road, Penn meets the innovators, researchers, communities and businesses pivoting to new energy sources and spearheading low-carbon technologies. In documentary segments, Penn speaks to the self-declared “crypto cowboys” of Texas who claim Bitcoin mining can help stabilize the state’s troubled electrical grid, and travels to Nevada to visit the company attempting to build America’s first closed-loop supply chain for electric vehicles. In New York, Penn explores the urban designs proposed to save the city from the next Superstorm Sandy and goes inside New York’s Empire State building to investigate the challenges of decarbonizing our cities and landmarks. 

The show builds on, and includes contributions from, Bloomberg Green’s award-winning team of climate journalists as well as London-based climate storytellers Jack Harries and Alice Aedy. With a focus on the most pressing questions for young viewers, Jack and Alice unpack one big idea each episode. From recycled wastewater to regenerative agriculture and the challenges of a just transition for workers in the energy sector, they’ll break down how countries across the world are finding intriguing solutions to our climate crisis, and outline the challenges ahead.

##### Transcript

###### Intro

**0:04** · Cooling, whether that's air conditioning or refrigerators is probably one of the biggest challenges we face with respect to climate change.

**0:13** · It's one of the least publicized threats in my view for all the progress we are making towards decarbonizing a broader energy system.

**0:24** · Global demand for air conditioning is predicted to triple by 2050.

**0:29** · Meeting that demand is a challenge that's at the heart of both the climate and cost of living crises around the world.

**0:36** · I think the problem is very rancid because we see the prices of electricity going up.

**0:41** · I don't think that low income population can cope with all these increased prices.

**0:46** · If everybody started to use air conditioning, for this we really need sustainable solutions to really take this forward.

**0:55** · So what else can we do to survive extraordinary heat without costing the environment?

**1:01** · Turns out some of the solutions already existed centuries ago.

###### Cool roofs

**1:10** · Dr. Denia Kolokotsa has been studying energy efficiency in buildings for the last three decades.

**1:17** · When I started doing this research everybody said that I was crazy.

**1:21** · You know, what are you going to do?

**1:23** · Now, I think everybody speaks about that.

**1:26** · So that's the difference.

**1:29** · Denia has studied a deceptively simple solution to our cooling problem.

**1:34** · Cool roofs.

**1:35** · Mainly that can be tiles, paints, shingles whatever it is attached within a roof that has the ability to reflect the sunlight and emit the thermal energy that is absorbed by the surfaces.

**1:52** · If it sounds a bit low tech to you that's probably the point.

**1:55** · This simple, yet effective solution has been around for centuries.

**1:59** · It's rooted in the concept of passive cooling used in ancient architecture.

**2:05** · For example, passive cooling in Cyclades in Greece is to paint the buildings white to emit the sun back to the sky.

**2:16** · Passive cooling in Egypt is to have smaller openings and smaller windows in order not to allow the sun to come in.

###### Madrids fish market

**2:27** · Madrid is notoriously hot in the summer.

**2:29** · That's a problem for Mercamadrid, the world's second biggest fish market.

**2:34** · It has the mammoth task of keeping thousands of workers and fish cool under its massive roof.

**2:53** · The market sells 172,000 tons of fish annually.

**3:10** · For example we were told this guy came all the way from Scotland.

**3:14** · Thanks to the cooling system, it's still alive.

**3:18** · Temperature inside the market used to get as high as 40 degrees Celsius, or 104 Fahrenheit, in the summer.

**3:25** · With thousands of people and fish sloshing in and out, keeping everything cold is a top priority.

**3:33** · In 2018, the market underwent a 3 million Euro makeover to do just that.

**3:51** · The entire roof was cleaned and repainted with a waterproof and highly reflective coating.

**4:08** · The project also added 68 evaporative cooling units to supply a constant stream of cold air into the market.

**4:33** · Mercamadrid says the new system saves up to 70% energy and cuts 34 tons of carbon emissions a year.

**4:41** · The temperature is now kept around 15 degrees Celsius, or about 60 degrees Fahrenheit, even on the hottest of summer days.

**4:58** · So cool roofs are helping this market, but in order to make a dent in the global demand for cooling we need multiple solutions working at once.

###### Skycool

**5:11** · In California, a company has come up with a new cooling technology that is also inspired by ancient wisdom.

**5:18** · About 10 years ago, I was finishing my PhD at Stanford and a labmate and I came across these references to a capability that apparently many ancient cultures had, which was the ability to make ice in the desert even though the air temperature was above freezing.

**5:36** · It turned out they were taking advantage of a natural phenomenon that's known as radiative cooling.

**5:44** · All objects, including you and I, and the walls around us actually emit our own heat away as a kind of light that we can't see.

**5:53** · So this light happens to be in the infrared part of the spectrum.

**5:57** · Now, if you go outside and look upwards our atmosphere actually lets out some of this light all the way out to outer space.

**6:06** · This effect was often known as night sky cooling or nocturnal cooling because it's really easy to observe at night.

**6:15** · We asked the question, why can't we make this passive cooling effect work during the daytime when we need cooling the most?

**6:24** · The co-founders of Skycool then developed a nano material to achieve this effect.

**6:30** · It's a class of materials that when you put them outside on a hot day, are actually cool to the touch.

**6:36** · It's not getting heated up by the sun but it's continuing to send that heat out upwards to the sky and space over those infrared wavelengths.

#### How America's hottest city is trying to cool down

**Vox**, *09 20, 2021*

##### Video (6:48)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/ZQ6fSHr5TJg title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Can trees help save Phoenix from extreme heat?

Subscribe and turn on notifications 🔔 so you don't miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

It’s time to stop looking at trees as a form of “beautification.” They are, instead, a living form of infrastructure, providing a variety of services that include stormwater management, air filtering, carbon sequestration, and, most importantly for a city like Phoenix, Arizona, they cool the environment around them. 

Trees can lower neighborhood temperatures in three ways: 
1) Their shade prevents solar radiation from hitting paved surfaces like concrete and asphalt, which absorb energy and rerelease it into the air as heat. 
2) Their leaves pull heat from the immediate area in order to evapotranspirate water that’s drawn from the soil. 
And, 3) If you’re standing under one, a tree protects your body directly from the sun’s rays. If you’ve ever made a summer visit to a dry, hot city like Phoenix, you’ll know how important shade is for making any outdoor experiences tolerable. 

As Phoenix deals with a rising frequency of extreme heat waves — which aren’t only deadly, but also cause worrisome spikes in energy demand — the city is looking to trees as part of its heat mitigation strategy. Phoenix isn’t devoid of trees, but they’re distributed unevenly across the city. A quick glance at a satellite image of the metro area reveals substantial green splotches in the north and east and brown ones in the south and west, where many lower-income neighborhoods are located. 

So Phoenix recently pledged to reach “tree equity” by 2030, under an agreement with American Forests, a national tree organization. I visited Phoenix recently to take a look at the current state of the city’s urban forest. In this video, we use drone imagery and thermal cameras to understand how the urban design of the city contributes to extreme heat, and what it can do to cool down. 

This is the first video of five videos we're releasing on climate change. You can watch the second video, about high-voltage transmission lines ⚡️ and why the US isn't ready for clean energy, here: https://youtu.be/s3ScJ_FwaZk

And the third video dives into prescribed burns, and how a decade of suppressing forest fires 🔥  may have made them worse, here: https://youtu.be/0o6ezu_h6iE

###### Intro

**0:01** · If you look at a thermal image of a city and then compare that to a map of vegetation, you'll find that where there's greenery, the temperature is lower.

**0:11** · That's because things like asphalt, concrete and shingled roofs absorb more heat from the sun than trees.

**0:19** · This is the urban heat island effect, and it accounts for the higher temperatures in cities, often by several degrees compared with their surroundings.

**0:28** · It's becoming a huge risk to human health as growing urban populations exacerbate the heating effects of climate change.

**0:36** · Heat waves kill more people than any other extreme weather event, more than tornadoes, hurricanes and even floods.

**0:47** · That's why urban heat island mitigation strategies are being studied in Singapore by a group of researchers.

**0:54** · The government-backed project called Cooling Singapore is now in the process of combining everything they've learned to create a digital tool that can help cities all over the world, starting with Singapore.

###### Cooling Singapore

**1:10** · In Singapore, close to the equator, temperatures regularly rise above 32 degrees Celsius or 90 degrees Fahrenheit.

**1:19** · And the city structures only make it worse.

**1:22** · And that is also the case for Singapore, which is basically a concrete jungle, more urbanized, more developed city.

**1:29** · And even in Singapore, what you have is a situation whereby there's a temperature difference of 7 degrees Celsius between the more urbanized and the more rural areas.

**1:41** · The government has taken drastic steps to keep temperatures down.

**1:46** · This is Gardens by the Bay, an award-winning park.

**1:50** · And inside this greenhouse it's a pleasant 24 degrees.

**1:54** · That's because the dome, along with two dozen nearby towers full of thousands of people, is chilled by what's probably the world's largest underground district cooling system.

**2:04** · It uses a large central plant that cools water and then pipes it into banks, residential towers, an exhibition center, shopping malls and the city's iconic Marina Bay Sands hotel and casino complex.

**2:18** · So one of the biggest perks of using this system for the buildings is that they can save 40% in terms of electricity usage compared to your traditional air conditioners.

**2:32** · And with Singapore relying on natural gas for most of its power, this new system means emissions savings equivalent to removing 10,000 cars from the city's roads.

**2:43** · That has big implications for the rest of the world.

**2:45** · If things stay as they are, more than a third of the world's electricity could end up being used to cool buildings and vehicles by 2050.

**2:55** · As the world gets hotter, gets warmer, there is a greater need for air conditioning and as well as refrigerators, for instance.

**3:03** · And the more people are buying these household appliances, the more energy usage they use and they release heat more, and that then exacerbates climate change.

**3:18** · It's a vicious circle.

###### Vegetation

**3:20** · And so since 2017, researchers at Cooling Singapore have been identifying design solutions that reduce our need for so much cool air in the first place.

**3:31** · One thing many cities have in common, and that's the importance of vegetation.

**3:36** · That's a very important measure to mitigate the urban heat because of the shading effect, of course, and deep psychological effects of the vegetation.

**3:46** · And also because of the possible evaporative cooling effect of the vegetation.

**3:53** · Vegetation can be, of course, on the ground floor in form of trees and shrubs.

**3:58** · And you can walk under them.

**4:00** · This is the so-called canopy layer that the vegetation forms above us.

**4:05** · But vegetation can also go up the facades of buildings and it can go to the roof of the buildings.

###### Garden City Feel

**4:14** · Luckily, Singapore has been striving for the Garden City feel for quite some time.

**4:20** · It was a vision initially introduced by then Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew in 1967 to make life more pleasant for people.

**4:28** · And today, Singapore is one of the world's greenest cities in terms of urban vegetation.

**4:33** · Kampung Admiralty, a community center that contains health facilities and social spaces, now provides more green space than the plot of land it was originally built on.

**4:44** · It's topped by a roofscape of staggered terraces covered in local plants, which functions as a community park, and a village green in the center that contains farm plots for residents to tend to.

**4:56** · Parkroyal on Pickering was designed as a hotel in a garden that doubled the green-growing potential of its site.

**5:04** · There's now 15,000 meters of sky gardens, reflecting pools, waterfalls, planter terraces and green walls.

**5:12** · And the government has big plans as well.

**5:17** · Singapore actually has a plan to plant 1 million trees and add more green spaces over the next 10 years.

**5:24** · It is actually a mix of one thing to reduce the urban heat island effect.

**5:30** · But on the other hand, it's also to to get the people to be more connected to nature.

**5:39** · But it's not enough.

###### Heat Mitigation

**5:41** · The city-state has still been warming twice as quickly as the world average over the past six decades.

**5:47** · That's why Cooling Singapore has developed a catalog of other potential heat-mitigation measures.

**5:54** · When you try to mitigate the urban heat island effect in a city or in any building, in a village as well, the first place to start is by shading of the windows.

**6:05** · You have to keep areas clear so that the wind can move through it.

**6:11** · Water of a certain depth can act as a very good thermal buffer.

**6:15** · If you have to construct heavy buildings, such as high rises, at least you can make the surface, the facade less heavy.

**6:24** · And you can protect it from direct sun penetration.

**6:27** · We have to make sure that no combustion engines will be in the city in the middle, in the medium- to long-term range.

**6:35** · So ideally, the electricity production is outside of the city.

**6:39** · And you bring just the clean electricity into the city.

**6:43** · You can at least minimize the use of energy in the city.

**6:48** · And you can start to slowly convert the roofs, the facades of the city, into production areas for renewable energy.

**6:58** · In Singapore, unfortunately, this is a limited option.

**7:01** · But in the long run, it could produce up to 20%, 25% of the energy, of the electricity needed in Singapore.

**7:10** · If all the roofs and the areas in the buildings, on the buildings, on the facades would be used to do that.

###### Urban Climate Twin

**7:20** · With so many different ideas, Cooling Singapore is also designing a virtual model of the city to test them out.

**7:26** · It's called a Digital Urban Climate Twin, or DUCT, that will calculate how each element of the city's design will impact the urban heat island effect.

**7:37** · That means we model not only the geometry of the buildings digitally, but also we model the transportation, the insulation, the temperature, the radiation coming from the sun, the weather, the local weather, the local climate, the even very, very microclimate of the city, the water, the movement of people in the city.

**8:01** · We can invent scenarios.

**8:04** · We can design scenarios, test them before we actually build them.

**8:09** · And if they test very well and we are sure that they will function, then we can start to build them and put them into reality.

###### Conclusion

**8:23** · Singapore will be using this new tool to figure out which actions it should take next.

**8:28** · And the model can be applied to any city, whether it needs to keep heat out or keep heat in, which will ultimately save energy, slow climate change and improve our quality of life.

**8:41** · So this is something that Singapore will be able to export, maybe even together with its city development systems that it already has.

**8:51** · Singapore is one of the very few cities in the world that really combined this scientific approach with a very well-established urban redesign and urban design approach.

**9:03** · Through its agencies and the combination of its agencies, it has achieved a lot in the past.

**9:10** · If it keeps following the scientific path and the combination with the other knowledge in the city already, we think that it will be a very comfortable and very livable city in the future, even more than today.

#### How systemic racism shaped the ecosystems of U.S. cities

**Science Magazine**, *10 09, 2020*

##### Transcript

**0:01** · The urban environment is a feat of human decision-making— from where to develop street grids lined with large glass office buildings, to which green spaces to preserve for outdoor recreation.

**0:13** · How humans make these choices, and the natural environment’s response, can create extremely different ecosystems in neighborhoods just a few blocks away from each other.

**0:23** · Researchers delved into dozens of studies to understand what drives these variations.

**0:29** · One well documented phenomenon in cities is the relationship between wealth and biodiversity.

**0:35** · More affluent areas generally have greater canopy cover, with larger, mature trees, as well as a higher diversity of birds.

**0:45** · This is known as the “luxury effect.”

**0:48** · Low-income areas typically have more man-made surfaces— including major heat-absorbers like asphalt and concrete, compared to higher-income areas.

**0:59** · The lack of shade from trees and vegetation, combined with more asphalt and concrete, makes it hotter in these neighborhoods— a phenomenon known as an “urban heat island.”

**1:10** · These communities are also more likely to be near sources of air pollutants, like expansive interstates pumping car exhaust.

**1:19** · Although wealth can sometimes predict the outcomes of an urban ecosystem, there isn’t always a clear relationship.

**1:26** · In some cases, the racial make-up of a neighborhood is better than income when forecasting canopy cover.

**1:33** · Researchers explored studies that highlight how systemic racism shaped our build environment.

**1:39** · One glaring example in the United States is residential segregation.

**1:44** · From 1933-1968, the federal government limited access to homeownership among Black Americans through a practice known as redlining.

**1:55** · Neighborhoods were graded based on the riskiness of providing a mortgage in the area.

**2:00** · The grades ranged from A, the most desirable areas, full of wealthy businessmen, to D, neighborhoods considered high-risk investments due to a combination of factors: from their environmental quality and distance from large industrial factories to the main determinant, the presence of foreign-born and Black people.

**2:22** · The inability for Black people to buy homes in these neighborhoods meant many types of capital investments left— landlords abandoned their properties, and public services, such as transportation and park maintenance, weren’t prioritized.

**2:36** · Today, many U.S. cities still exhibit long-lasting environmental impacts from this discrimination.

**2:42** · Neighborhoods which had a “D” grade in the 60s have about half the canopy cover of historically white communities.

**2:50** · Some studies evaluate how the current environment relates to historically redlined communities, but researchers did not find any research that traces how ecosystems changed over time because of this segregation.

**3:03** · They propose that because habitable regions are more spread out in these areas, animal populations struggle to breed since they are cut off from each other.

**3:14** · The reduced breeding options for animals could have decreased gene diversity, an important way for animals to adapt to changing environments.

**3:23** · And decreased gene flow of native species could promote the abundance of pest species, like mosquitos and brown rats, which carry diseases that can infect humans.

**3:34** · The combination of all these outcomes— from urban heat islands to increased pests— make low-income, marginalized communities far more vulnerable to risks like climate change.

**3:47** · Scientists say such evidence shows that conservation and social justice cross paths— especially along neighborhood streets.

Check out our Patreon: https://www.patreon.com/cw/PBSWeathered?utm_medium=unknown&utm_source=join_link&utm_campaign=creatorshare_creator&utm_content=copyLink 

Heat is the deadliest weather hazard in the U.S. and many places around the world, and it's only getting worse.

The most deadly heat waves so far have been dry heat waves. But a new threat is rising: humid heat waves, aka wet-bulb events. Scientists have identified wet-bulb temperatures where sweat can’t evaporate fast enough to cool the human body. And once this threshold is crossed, it doesn’t matter how much shade or water you have: you won’t survive without environmental cooling like air conditioning.

In this episode of Weathered, we break down: What wet-bulb temperature actually means, why it’s so dangerous, what areas will be affected, and why air conditioning, while essential, isn’t enough.

###### Intro

**0:00** · Search Google Earth for China and you’ll see this.

**0:03** · But an unedited satellite photo might look more like this.

**0:13** · But it’s not only here.

**0:14** · In cities around the world, air pollution is a big problem.

**0:18** · A majority of humans now live in cities and that number is only going to rise, which means more cars, more factories, and more power plants.

**0:25** · As officials explore options for fighting air pollution, there is one tool that is often overlooked: trees.

###### Air pollution

**0:35** · Cities are centers of industry, but the resulting pollution is filling our lungs and making us sick.

**0:41** · One major culprit is particulate matter: airborne particles of dust, soot and smoke that are released when we burn fossil fuels or kicked up during construction and farming.

**0:49** · When we inhale them, they can cause asthma and they can also enter our bloodstream to cause strokes and even death.

**0:54** · Experts estimate that outdoor air pollution kills over three million people a year and as cities grow, leaders are funding creative—and often expensive—solutions for the problem.

**1:04** · In London, the mayor spent over a million pounds spraying city streets with an adhesive that was supposed to glue pollutants to the road.

**1:10** · and in the Netherlands, designers have created a giant air purifier they call "The Smog Free Tower", which is cool, but there is another, simpler solution… A new report from The Nature Conservancy shows that planting trees can be a cost-effective way to improve public health, which they do in two ways: First, a tree removes particulate matter when polluted air blows through its branches.

###### Planting trees

**1:31** · The particulate matter settles on the leaves and when it rains the dust is washed down the gutter so we don’t inhale it.

**1:37** · Second, trees cool temperatures by providing shade and releasing water through photosynthesis, which cools summer temperatures by about two to four degrees fahrenheit.

**1:46** · But there is a catch!

**1:47** · Trees can only clean and cool the air within a close radius: about one hundred feet, so city officials need to be careful where they plant.

**1:54** · Officials can maximize pollution reduction by planting trees where population density and air pollution overlap.

**1:59** · The Nature Conservancy report uses data from Washington D.C. to create a map showing where planting trees will have the highest return on investment.

**2:06** · And some trees work better than others: trees with larger, stickier leaves, like maples and elms are more effective, but they also need to be considered within the larger ecosystem.

**2:15** · Compared to DC, many cities around the world have even more to gain from planting trees: this map shows where return on investment is highest for reducing particulate matter.

**2:23** · With proper targeting, planting trees can be just as cost-effective as other strategies like converting public transportation to use less diesel fuel.

**2:30** · But there is one major limiting factor: water access.

**2:34** · What might work in Boston, will be less feasible in a city like Doha, Qatar, where water is a scarce resource.

**2:39** · And on top of that, many mayors don’t yet think of trees as a public health resource.

**2:44** · Trees might not look like giant air filters, but that’s exactly what they are, and the sooner we start thinking of them that way, the sooner the air we breathe might be cooler and cleaner in cities around the world.

**0:04** · There’s a reason that summers in the city are so hot, and it’s probably easiest to explain why with thermal vision.

**0:11** · It shows the heat all around me and also the coldness of this ice cream cone.

**0:16** · Cities are often hotter than their suburbs due to a phenomenon known as “the heat island effect.”

###### The Heat Island Effect

**0:24** · All of that asphalt, concrete, dark rooftops and tall buildings— they absorb and store heat.

**0:31** · And there are a lot of people using a lot of energy— driving cars, riding subways, running the AC.

**0:38** · All of these materials and activities either create or retain heat.

**0:44** · And all that stored heat causes steeper nighttime highs … when people would otherwise have a chance to cool down.

**0:52** · The way all these heat-storing elements are laid out matters quite a bit.

**0:57** · In cities laid out in grids, like Phoenix, Chicago, or Washington, D.C., the buildings are closer together, like closely packed coals in a fire, keeping heat in.

**1:07** · More space between buildings creates more circulation.

**1:11** · Another way to combat this heat island effect is through green space.

**1:15** · Parks, trees, plants— they don’t absorb as much heat … they actually send water back in the atmosphere.

**1:21** · Between all those hot buildings, that cools things off.

**1:25** · Another solution is color.

###### Color Light

**1:27** · Light colors reflect sunlight back into the atmosphere instead of storing it as heat.

**1:31** · It's easiest to see in crosswalks, and it's true for the color of buildings and other urban surfaces, too.

**1:39** · And one long-game way to combat the heat island effect is to avoid using air conditioning when you don’t need it.

###### Avoid Using Air Conditioning

**1:45** · AC uses a ton of electricity and creates a feedback loop.

**1:49** · When we get that electricity from coal or natural gas, that puts more carbon dioxide into the atmosphere … which warms the planet … making cities even hotter.

**2:00** · But this isn’t just about comfort.

##### Description

Filmed during the hottest days of Phoenix, Arizona’s summer heatwave, A NEW INFERNO follows paramedics as they race to save the lives of heatstroke victims using a radical new treatment: ice immersion therapy.  As featured on the NY Times Op Docs — We Are Living in a New Inferno  World Premiere SXSW Film Festival, 2026  Featuring Jason Smith, Jake West, Roy Lewis, & Colter Fosdick Directed & Produced by Nita Blum-Reddick & Jonathan Pickett Executive Producers Sam Osborn, Alejandra Vasquez, & Jesse Ray Sheps Cinematographer Ryan Dent  Editor Jonathan Pickett  Composer Jack Gillette Production Sound Mixer Daniel Reddick  Grips Stephane Strande & Brian Osback Sound Design & Mix Hansdale Hsu Colorist Keyhan Bayegan Production Assistant Camden Smith Title & Poster Designer Jason Cryer Weather Consultant Jorge Torres Advisors Dr. Charles Finch, Medical Director, Phoenix Fire Department & Maki Lloyd, Deputy Chief, Phoenix Fire Department  For The New York Times Op-Docs: Associate Producers Ingrid Homquist & Rebecca Shaid Producer Yvonne Ashley Kouadjo Senior Producer Andrew Blackwell Executive Producer Alexandra Garcia  Please consider supporting the ongoing work of Circle the City: www.circlethecity.org  Festivals: • Tribeca x NYT Op-Docs • Mountainfilm • Rooftop Films • Palm Springs International ShortFest • Indy Shorts Film Festival • HollyShorts Film Festival • Nashville Film Festival • Bend Film Festival • Mill Valley Film Festival • Sidewalk Film Festival • deadCenter Film Festival • Ouray International Film Festival • Cinema Columbus • AfterImage Film Festival • Coast Film Festival
